notes.front: The Guide says the Scrum Master leads, trains and coaches the organisation in its Scrum adoption. What is an organisation’s Scrum adoption?
notes.back: The organisation’s taking up of Scrum, which the Scrum Master serves by leading, training and coaching it.
notes.explanation: The Guide puts this first among the ways the Scrum Master serves the organisation, beside planning and advising Scrum implementations.
notes.example: Like a sports club switching to a new set of rules: someone has to lead the change and teach and coach everyone in the club, not just one team’s players.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: The Scrum Master serves the organisation by {{c1::leading, training, and coaching}} the organisation in its Scrum adoption.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Master’s reach goes beyond the Scrum Team: three verbs describe how the whole organisation is helped to take up Scrum.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: The Scrum Master serves the organisation by {{c1::planning and advising}} Scrum implementations within the organisation.
notes.explanation: Beyond coaching, the Guide gives the Scrum Master a hand in how Scrum is put in place across the organisation.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: The Scrum Master serves the organisation by helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact {{c1::an empirical approach for complex work}}.
notes.explanation: The help is aimed at people outside the Scrum Team too, and at doing as well as understanding.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: Are the four listed ways the only ways the Scrum Master serves the organisation?
notes.back: No: the Guide says “in several ways, including”, so the list is open.
notes.explanation: The Guide names four examples without closing the list, so other help to the organisation also fits the role.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: Why does the Scrum Guide not describe the patterns, processes and insights found while using Scrum?
notes.back: They are context sensitive and differ widely between Scrum uses, so they are described elsewhere.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines the framework only, leaving tactics for particular situations to other sources.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Purpose of the Scrum Guide”
notes.evidence: Their description is beyond the purpose of the Scrum Guide because they are context sensitive and differ widely between Scrum uses. Such tactics for using within the Scrum framework vary widely and are described elsewhere.

notes.front: Scrum is being adopted in many domains holding essentially complex work, beyond {{c1::software product development}}, where it has its roots.
notes.explanation: As its use spreads, researchers, analysts, scientists and other specialists do the work, not only software developers.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Purpose of the Scrum Guide”
notes.evidence: We are humbled to see Scrum being adopted in many domains holding essentially complex work, beyond software product development where Scrum has its roots. As Scrum’s use spreads, developers, researchers, analysts, scientists, and other specialists do the work. We use the word “developers” in Scrum not to exclude, but to simplify.

notes.front: Why does the Guide use the word “developers” for everyone who does the work, whatever their specialism?
notes.back: Not to exclude, but to simplify.
notes.explanation: Researchers, analysts, scientists and other specialists all count as developers in Scrum.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Purpose of the Scrum Guide”
notes.evidence: We are humbled to see Scrum being adopted in many domains holding essentially complex work, beyond software product development where Scrum has its roots. As Scrum’s use spreads, developers, researchers, analysts, scientists, and other specialists do the work. We use the word “developers” in Scrum not to exclude, but to simplify.

notes.front: Scrum is simple. Try it {{c1::as is}} and determine if its philosophy, theory, and structure help to achieve goals and create value.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks for an honest trial of the whole framework before judging whether it helps.
notes.evidence: Scrum is simple. Try it as is and determine if its philosophy, theory, and structure help to achieve goals and create value.

notes.front: Leadership wants to introduce Scrum in five more departments next year and asks the Scrum Master what to do. Which response fits the Scrum Master’s service to the organisation?
notes.back: D) Work with leadership to plan and advise the Scrum implementations.
notes.choices:
A) Become the manager of the new teams
B) Decline, since the Scrum Master serves only one Scrum Team
C) Hand leadership a copy of the Guide and step back
D) Work with leadership to plan and advise the Scrum implementations
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says Scrum Masters serve the larger organisation too. C: the Scrum Master leads, trains and coaches the adoption, not just hands over a document. A: the Guide gives the Scrum Master no management role over teams.
notes.explanation: Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organisation is one of the ways the Guide says the Scrum Master serves it.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: Managers across the company keep asking Scrum Teams for detailed status reports because they do not understand how Scrum works. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: C) Lead, train and coach the managers as part of the organisation’s Scrum adoption.
notes.choices:
A) Write the reports for the managers each week
B) Tell the teams to ignore the managers
C) Lead, train and coach the managers as part of the organisation’s Scrum adoption
D) Ask the Product Owner to deal with it
notes.choicesExplained: A: this keeps the misunderstanding in place. B: ignoring the managers leaves the barrier standing. D: serving the organisation in its Scrum adoption is named as the Scrum Master’s service.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the Scrum Master serves the organisation by leading, training and coaching it in its Scrum adoption.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: The finance department insists every product commit to fixed annual scope before funding. What fits the Scrum Master’s service to the organisation?
notes.back: D) Help finance staff understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work.
notes.choices:
A) Accept the fixed scope and pad every estimate
B) Tell finance that Scrum forbids budgets
C) Leave finance to the Product Owner and stay with the team
D) Help finance staff understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work
notes.choicesExplained: A: padding still fixes the plan instead of learning from results. B: the Guide says nothing against budgets. C: the Guide lists helping employees and stakeholders with an empirical approach among the Scrum Master’s services to the organisation.
notes.explanation: Empiricism holds that knowledge comes from experience and decisions from what is observed, which a scope fixed a year ahead cannot use.
notes.evidence: Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking. Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed.

notes.front: Customers’ feedback reaches the Scrum Team only through three layers of managers, weeks late. What should the Scrum Master work on?
notes.back: D) Removing the barriers between stakeholders and the Scrum Team.
notes.choices:
A) Adding a fourth layer to speed things up
B) Telling the team to wait for the managers
C) Collecting all feedback personally and filtering it
D) Removing the barriers between stakeholders and the Scrum Team
notes.choicesExplained: A: another layer adds delay. B: waiting leaves the barrier in place. C: the Scrum Master would become another barrier.
notes.explanation: Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams is one of the ways the Scrum Master serves the organisation.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: A Scrum Team has grown to sixteen people. Its Daily Scrum overruns and communication suffers. What might the Scrum Master suggest the team consider?
notes.back: A) Reorganising into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product.
notes.choices:
A) Reorganising into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product
B) Extending the Daily Scrum to one hour
C) Appointing team leads to report to the Scrum Master
D) Splitting into a team of builders and a team of testers
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Daily Scrum is 15 minutes. C: there are no sub-teams or hierarchies in a Scrum Team. D: each Scrum Team should be cross-functional and cohesive, not split by skill.
notes.explanation: The Guide says teams that become too large should consider this, and that smaller teams in general communicate better.
notes.evidence: If Scrum Teams become too large, they should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product. Therefore, they should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

notes.front: A large product is split into three Scrum Teams. A manager proposes that each team gets its own Product Backlog and Product Goal. What should the Scrum Master advise?
notes.back: C) Teams focused on the same product should share one Product Goal and one Product Backlog.
notes.choices:
A) Agree: three teams need three backlogs
B) Keep one backlog but give each team its own Product Goal
C) Teams focused on the same product should share one Product Goal and one Product Backlog
D) Let each team decide separately
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: separate backlogs split a single product. B: the teams should share the Product Goal too.
notes.explanation: The Guide says multiple cohesive Scrum Teams on the same product should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner.
notes.evidence: If Scrum Teams become too large, they should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product. Therefore, they should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

notes.front: The same three teams are about to be given a Product Owner each for their shared product. What should the Scrum Master point out?
notes.back: A) Teams on the same product should share the same Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) Teams on the same product should share the same Product Owner
B) The Scrum Master should act as Product Owner for two teams
C) Three Product Owners are needed for three teams
D) The Product Owners should form a committee
notes.choicesExplained: C: the Guide says the teams share the Product Owner. B: the Scrum Master is not the Product Owner. D: the Product Owner is one person, not a committee.
notes.explanation: One product keeps one Product Owner accountable for its value, whatever the number of Scrum Teams.
notes.evidence: If Scrum Teams become too large, they should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product. Therefore, they should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

notes.front: The head of a marketing department asks whether Scrum could work for them, since they “don’t build software”. How should the Scrum Master answer?
notes.back: C) Scrum is used in many domains of complex work beyond software; they could try it as is.
notes.choices:
A) No: Scrum is only for software
B) Only if they rename marketers as programmers
C) Scrum is used in many domains of complex work beyond software; they could try it as is
D) Only after they hire software developers
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide describes Scrum spreading to many complex domains. B and D: the Guide uses “developers” for anyone doing the work, not to exclude.
notes.explanation: The Guide notes Scrum’s adoption beyond software product development, where it has its roots.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Purpose of the Scrum Guide”
notes.evidence: We are humbled to see Scrum being adopted in many domains holding essentially complex work, beyond software product development where Scrum has its roots. As Scrum’s use spreads, developers, researchers, analysts, scientists, and other specialists do the work. We use the word “developers” in Scrum not to exclude, but to simplify.

notes.front: A team asks the Scrum Master where in the Scrum Guide it explains how to write backlog items and estimate them. What is the right answer?
notes.back: C) The Guide does not describe such tactics; they are context sensitive and described elsewhere.
notes.choices:
A) In the Scrum Master section
B) In the Product Backlog section, which prescribes one format
C) The Guide does not describe such tactics; they are context sensitive and described elsewhere
D) Nowhere, because Scrum forbids estimation
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide prescribes no item format. A: the Scrum Master section describes services, not techniques. D: the Guide says the Developers are responsible for sizing.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines the framework and leaves context-sensitive patterns, processes and insights to other sources.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Purpose of the Scrum Guide”
notes.evidence: Their description is beyond the purpose of the Scrum Guide because they are context sensitive and differ widely between Scrum uses. Such tactics for using within the Scrum framework vary widely and are described elsewhere.

notes.front: Before ever running a Sprint, a new department plans to drop the Sprint Retrospective and merge the Product Owner into the manager role. What should the Scrum Master advise?
notes.back: A) Try Scrum as is first and determine whether it helps achieve goals and create value.
notes.choices:
A) Try Scrum as is first and determine whether it helps achieve goals and create value
B) Make the changes; every department is different
C) Adopt only the Daily Scrum to start with
D) Wait until another department proves Scrum works
notes.choicesExplained: B: changing Scrum’s elements covers up problems and limits its benefits. C: implementing only parts of Scrum means the result is not Scrum. D: the Guide asks each group to try it and judge the result.
notes.explanation: The Guide invites people to try Scrum as is and judge from the result; dropping an element, now or later, covers up problems and leaves a result that is not Scrum.
notes.evidence: Scrum is simple. Try it as is and determine if its philosophy, theory, and structure help to achieve goals and create value.

notes.front: After adopting Scrum, a director complains: “Scrum has made our approval process look slow, so Scrum is the problem.” What should the Scrum Master help the director see?
notes.back: C) Scrum makes visible how well current management and work techniques perform, so that improvements can be made.
notes.choices:
A) Scrum should be paused until approvals are faster
B) The approval process is outside Scrum, so it is irrelevant
C) Scrum makes visible how well current management and work techniques perform, so that improvements can be made
D) The teams should skip approvals
notes.choicesExplained: A: pausing Scrum hides the problem again. B: the Guide says Scrum shows the efficacy of current management too. D: bypassing the process does not improve it.
notes.explanation: The Guide says Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of current management, environment and work techniques.
notes.evidence: Scrum wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary. Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of current management, environment, and work techniques, so that improvements can be made.

notes.front: A department head wants to appoint a lead inside the Scrum Team who assigns work to the other Developers and reports on them. What should the Scrum Master explain?
notes.back: D) Within a Scrum Team there are no sub-teams or hierarchies.
notes.choices:
A) A lead is fine if the lead is a senior Developer
B) The Scrum Master should become the lead
C) The lead should report to the Product Owner
D) Within a Scrum Team there are no sub-teams or hierarchies
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: seniority or the Scrum Master role does not create a hierarchy the Guide allows. C: reporting lines to the Product Owner are still a hierarchy.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes a Scrum Team as a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective, the Product Goal.
notes.evidence: Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies. It is a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal.

notes.front: The organisation wants the Scrum Team only to write code; testing, operation and maintenance are handed to other departments. What should the Scrum Master help leaders understand?
notes.back: B) The Scrum Team is responsible for all product-related activities and is structured and empowered by the organisation to manage its work.
notes.choices:
A) Hand-offs are fine as long as they are fast
B) The Scrum Team is responsible for all product-related activities and is structured and empowered by the organisation to manage its work
C) The Scrum Master should manage the hand-offs
D) Only the Product Owner may decide team structure
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide gives the Scrum Team all product-related activities. C: managing hand-offs keeps the split in place. D: the Guide says the organisation structures and empowers the team.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists verification, maintenance and operation among the Scrum Team’s product-related activities.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team is responsible for all product-related activities from stakeholder collaboration, verification, maintenance, operation, experimentation, research and development, and anything else that might be required. They are structured and empowered by the organization to manage their own work.

notes.front: The organisation has a standard Definition of Done. One Scrum Team wants to drop two of its criteria to go faster. What should the Scrum Master say?
notes.back: C) Where the Definition of Done is an organisational standard, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum.
notes.choices:
A) The team may relax it if the Product Owner agrees
B) The team may relax it for one Sprint
C) Where the Definition of Done is an organisational standard, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum
D) The Scrum Master may approve exceptions
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D: no one in the Guide can take a team below the organisation’s minimum.
notes.explanation: A team may add to the organisation’s standard but not go below it.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum.

notes.front: Three Scrum Teams on one product each keep a different Definition of Done, and their work often fails to fit together. What should the Scrum Master help them do?
notes.back: D) Mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.
notes.choices:
A) Keep their own definitions and test together at the end
B) Let the strictest team decide for the others
C) Drop the Definition of Done until integration is fixed
D) Mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done
notes.choicesExplained: A: separate definitions are what the Guide rules out. B: the Guide says the teams define it mutually. C: work cannot be part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product to share one Definition of Done.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”
notes.evidence: If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

notes.front: Senior executives keep reversing the Product Owner’s ordering decisions after each Sprint Review. What should the Scrum Master help the organisation understand?
notes.back: C) For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organisation must respect their decisions.
notes.choices:
A) Executives outrank the Product Owner, so their changes stand
B) The Scrum Master should arbitrate each disagreement
C) For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organisation must respect their decisions
D) The Product Owner should stop holding Sprint Reviews
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide asks the whole organisation to respect the Product Owner’s decisions. B: the Scrum Master does not decide backlog order. D: dropping an event loses an opportunity to inspect and adapt.
notes.explanation: The Product Owner’s decisions show in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog; executives who disagree can try to convince the Product Owner.
notes.evidence: For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions. These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog, and through the inspectable Increment at the Sprint Review.

notes.front: Staff in another department believe “empirical” means Scrum Teams work with no plans at all. How can the Scrum Master best help?
notes.back: A) Explain that empiricism means decisions based on experience and what is observed, and help them enact that approach.
notes.choices:
A) Explain that empiricism means decisions based on experience and what is observed, and help them enact that approach
B) Agree: Scrum Teams do not plan
C) Tell them empiricism only concerns the Developers
D) Give them a fixed yearly plan to reassure them
notes.choicesExplained: B: Scrum has Sprint Planning and a Product Backlog. C: the Guide names helping employees and stakeholders with an empirical approach as a service to the organisation. D: a fixed plan works against empiricism.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines empiricism as knowledge coming from experience and decisions based on what is observed, which still involves planning.
notes.evidence: Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking. Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed.

notes.front: A senior manager tells the Scrum Master: “Just coach your team; the rest of the organisation is not your concern.” What does the Guide say?
notes.back: B) The Scrum Master helps everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, within the Scrum Team and the organisation.
notes.choices:
A) The manager is right: the Scrum Master serves only the Scrum Team
B) The Scrum Master helps everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, within the Scrum Team and the organisation
C) The Scrum Master serves the organisation only if the team has no impediments
D) Only the Product Owner deals with the organisation
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide lists services to the organisation as well. C: the Guide sets no such condition. D: the Guide gives the Scrum Master its own services to the organisation.
notes.explanation: The Guide ties the Scrum Master’s accountability for establishing Scrum to helping the whole organisation understand it, not only the team.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide. They do this by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, both within the Scrum Team and the organization.

notes.front: In the Guide, “removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams” is a way the Scrum Master serves whom?
notes.back: C) The organisation.
notes.choices:
A) The Scrum Team
B) The Product Owner
C) The organisation
D) The stakeholders only
notes.choicesExplained: A: the team list covers self-management, Done Increments, impediments and events. B: the Product Owner list has facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed. D: the Guide has no separate list for stakeholders.
notes.explanation: It appears with Scrum adoption, Scrum implementations and an empirical approach for complex work in the organisation list.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: In the Guide, “planning and advising Scrum implementations” is a way the Scrum Master serves whom?
notes.back: A) The organisation.
notes.choices:
A) The organisation
B) The Product Owner
C) The Scrum Team
D) The Developers
notes.choicesExplained: D and C: the team list covers coaching, Done Increments, impediments and events. B: the Product Owner list covers backlog techniques, clear items, empirical product planning and stakeholder collaboration.
notes.explanation: Implementations happen “within the organization”, and the item sits in the organisation list beside leading its Scrum adoption.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the organization in several ways, including: - Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption; - Planning and advising Scrum implementations within the organization; - Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work; and, - Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

notes.front: Research scientists joining a Scrum Team object that they are “not developers” and so do not belong at the Daily Scrum. What should the Scrum Master explain?
notes.back: D) Scrum uses “developers” not to exclude but to simplify; anyone doing the work is a Developer.
notes.choices:
A) They should attend only the Sprint Review
B) They are right: only programmers attend
C) They should form a separate research sub-team
D) Scrum uses “developers” not to exclude but to simplify; anyone doing the work is a Developer
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says the word is not meant to exclude. C: a Scrum Team has no sub-teams. A: those doing the work are Developers, and the Daily Scrum is their event.
notes.explanation: The Guide names researchers, analysts, scientists and other specialists among those doing the work in Scrum.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Purpose of the Scrum Guide”
notes.evidence: We are humbled to see Scrum being adopted in many domains holding essentially complex work, beyond software product development where Scrum has its roots. As Scrum’s use spreads, developers, researchers, analysts, scientists, and other specialists do the work. We use the word “developers” in Scrum not to exclude, but to simplify.

notes.front: Leadership proposes to “adopt Scrum” by renaming project managers as Scrum Masters and keeping everything else as it is. How should the Scrum Master advise them?
notes.back: B) Plan a real adoption: try Scrum as is, with its accountabilities, events and artifacts, and judge the results.
notes.choices:
A) Agree: the names are what make it Scrum
B) Plan a real adoption: try Scrum as is, with its accountabilities, events and artifacts, and judge the results
C) Rename the teams too and call it done
D) Refuse to discuss adoption until the teams ask
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: renaming changes nothing the Guide defines. D: planning and advising Scrum implementations is part of the Scrum Master’s service to the organisation.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks people to try Scrum as is and determine if it helps, which renaming alone does not test.
notes.evidence: Scrum is simple. Try it as is and determine if its philosophy, theory, and structure help to achieve goals and create value.
